claims.text: A machine-learning framework trained on historical composition–process–structure–property data can predict optimal heat-treatment profiles for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Machine-learning-predicted heat treatments can control phase evolution more reliably than traditional trial-and-error approaches.
The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has a mixed or transitional phase microstructure after conventional processing.
The ML-predicted profiles specify targeted temperatures, pressures, and cooling rates.
Precisely controlled temperature, atmosphere, and programmed cooling permit reproducible maintenance of treatment variables.
Relevant constituent phases may include B2, A2, FCC, and other ordered domains.
The formation and morphology of constituent phases mediate the alloy's mechanical and functional properties.
Large historical datasets allow an ML model to capture complex interactions among composition, processing conditions, and microstructure.
Prediction of sensitive heat-treatment parameters can guide nucleation and growth kinetics toward a desirable phase distribution.
ML-guided samples will have a higher fraction of the desired phases than conventionally treated samples.
ML-guided samples will exhibit more controlled phase morphology than conventionally treated samples.
The modified phase fraction and morphology will produce improved or targeted mechanical or functional properties.
Manual iterative heat-treatment selection lacks systematic predictive power.
The success of the ML approach depends on the quality and breadth of the historical data.
Application outside the model's trained composition or processing regimes may require further refinement.
Advanced computational tools are useful because the HEA compositional space is too large for systematic experimental screening.
The achievable degree of phase control and property enhancement under varied practical conditions remains uncertain.
A controlled comparison using quantitative phase analysis, microscopy, and mechanical testing can test the proposed improvement.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in both targeted phase fractions and corresponding properties would falsify the hypothesis.
